subject: Architecture
title: Urban Heat Islands: Cities That Cook
description: A short lesson to help you apply Urban Heat Islands: Cities That Cook.

hook.text: Cities can be 10°F hotter than surrounding countryside — concrete, steel, and asphalt absorb and radiate heat.

buildup.text: Dark roofs, parking lots, and roads soak up sunlight. At night, they release stored heat instead of cooling down.

discovery.text: Removing trees for development eliminates natural cooling — each mature tree provides the same cooling as ten AC units.

twist.text: Air conditioning exhaust makes it worse — units dump indoor heat outdoors, raising street temperatures further.

climax.text: Los Angeles now paints streets with reflective coating. Cool roofs and urban forests are spreading worldwide.

punchline.text: We built cities that cook themselves. Now we're learning to cool them down.

quiz.question: Why are cities hotter than surrounding rural areas?
options: More people generate body heat in dense populations
Concrete and asphalt absorb and radiate heat instead of cooling
Tall buildings block wind and trap warm air at street level

details.summary: Urban heat islands form when dark pavement, concrete buildings, and lack of vegetation trap and radiate solar heat, making cities 3-8°C hotter than surrounding countryside. As climate change worsens, this architectural phenomenon turns some neighborhoods into lethal heat traps during extreme events.
details.whyItMatters: Urban heat islands kill more people than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. Architecture created this problem through material choices and urban form — and architecture must solve it through cool roofs, trees, and redesigned public spaces.
takeaways: Cities can be 3-8°C hotter than surrounding countryside
Dark pavement and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat
Heat islands kill more people than most natural disasters

faq.question: What causes urban heat islands?
faq.answer: Dark surfaces (asphalt, dark roofs) absorb solar energy and re-radiate it as heat. Tall buildings trap heat between them and block cooling winds. Lack of vegetation eliminates evaporative cooling. Air conditioning exhaust adds heat. The result: cities become self-heating ovens.

faq.question: How can architecture reduce urban heat?
faq.answer: Cool (reflective) roofs, green roofs with vegetation, permeable light-colored pavements, urban tree canopy, water features, and building orientations that channel breezes. Los Angeles has painted streets white and mandated cool roofs, reducing local temperatures measurably.
